learn.hook: Is there a magic trick that turns a tiny seed into a mango tree overnight? Let's find out!
points: The lesson 'A Bottle of Dew' is a story about wanting quick success and learning the value of hard work.
A shortcut promises fast results with little effort; hard work means steady effort over time.
To understand a story, ask: Who is in it? What do they want? What problem do they face? How does it end?
The moral of a story is the lesson it teaches. We find it by looking at what happens to the characters because of their choices.
Read every question carefully and look back at the passage for the exact words that prove your answer.

example.q: Read this passage: Meera wanted the best mangoes in the village. Her friend Kabir said, "Just buy a magic powder and the tree will fruit overnight!" Meera shook her head. Every morning she watered her little tree, pulled out weeds and added compost. Two summers later, her tree gave sweet, golden mangoes, and she shared them with everyone. What lesson does the story teach?
steps: Meera's goal: to grow the best mangoes.
Kabir offers a shortcut: a 'magic powder'.
Meera chooses steady work: watering, weeding and adding compost every day.
Result: after two summers, her tree gives sweet mangoes.
So the story shows that patient hard work brings real results.
example.answer: Patient, steady hard work brings real success; shortcuts rarely do.

learn.reallife: Practising cricket in the nets every evening, or revising a little every day before exams, works better than hoping for a last-minute trick.

games.title: True or false: Meera's story

quiz.q: Meera "watered her little tree, pulled out weeds and added compost" every morning. This shows that Meera was:

options: Good results can take a long time

quiz.mistake: Mixes up Kabir's promise with what really happened

options: Steady hard work brings real success

quiz.explain: Sharing your mangoes with everyone is a generous act.

quiz.explain: The story is about patient work leading to sweet mangoes, so 'Sweet Fruit of Patience' sums it up.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a title based on a small detail rather than the main idea

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: 'Why not just use a shortcut? Why did Meera work so hard on her tree?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Slow and steady effort gives real results. I'll practise my flying every day!
teach.nudge: But what did Meera get in the end because of her effort?

learn.hook: Words like 'honest', 'patient' and 'greedy' are tiny labels that tell us what a person is really like inside.
points: Values are good qualities that guide how we behave: honesty, patience, kindness, hard work, sharing.
Synonyms are words with similar meanings: hard-working = diligent; patient = calm while waiting.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: honest ↔ dishonest, patient ↔ impatient, generous ↔ selfish.
The prefixes 'un-', 'im-' and 'dis-' can make opposites: kind → unkind, patient → impatient, honest → dishonest.
We judge characters by what they say and do, not just by what they are called.

example.q: Think it through: Arjun finds a ₹100 note in the school corridor and hands it to his teacher. Which value does he show, and what is its opposite?
steps: Arjun does not keep money that isn't his.
Returning lost things shows honesty.
Adding 'dis-' to 'honest' gives its opposite.
example.answer: Honesty; the opposite word is 'dishonest'.

learn.reallife: When you return a friend's lost pencil box or wait calmly in the lunch queue, you are showing values in action.

games.title: Good value or not?
buckets: Does not show a good value

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'hard-working'?
quiz.explain: 'Diligent' means working carefully and steadily, just like 'hard-working'.
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: What is the antonym of 'patient'?
quiz.explain: We add the prefix 'im-' to 'patient' to make 'impatient'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong prefix to form the opposite

quiz.q: Choose the opposite of 'honest'.
quiz.explain: The opposite of 'honest' is formed with 'dis-': dishonest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every word takes 'un-' to make its opposite

quiz.q: Riya gives half of her laddoos to a friend who forgot his tiffin. Which value does she show?
quiz.explain: Giving away part of what you have to help someone is generosity.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a good value with a bad quality

quiz.q: Which sentence shows patience?
options: Sonu pushed others to get on the swing.
Sonu shouted because the swing was busy.
Sonu broke the swing in anger.
Sonu waited calmly for his turn on the swing.
quiz.explain: Waiting calmly for your turn is what patience means.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the action with the value of patience

quiz.q: Which word is the antonym of 'generous'?
quiz.explain: A generous person shares; a selfish person keeps everything for himself or herself.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a synonym instead of the opposite

quiz.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'kind'?
quiz.explain: 'Kind' becomes 'unkind'. 'Re-' means 'again', not 'not'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'dis-' or 're-' without checking the real word

quiz.q: A 'shortcut' in a story usually means:
options: a quick, easy way that skips the real effort
quiz.explain: In stories about hard work, a shortcut is a way to get results quickly without doing the work.
quiz.mistake: Takes only the literal meaning of the word

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'What are values? And how do I make the opposite of a word like honest?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Values are good qualities, and little prefixes like 'dis-' and 'un-' flip a word into its opposite!
teach.nudge: And how can I turn 'honest' into its opposite word?

topics.title: Telling a story in the simple past

learn.hook: Most stories begin with 'Once upon a time...' and then the verbs travel back in time!
points: Stories usually use the simple past tense because they tell about things that already happened.
Regular verbs add -ed or -d: walk → walked, water → watered, smile → smiled.
Irregular verbs change in their own way: go → went, buy → bought, give → gave, see → saw.
Negative: did not + base verb ('She did not buy the powder', not 'did not bought').
Question: Did + subject + base verb ('Did Meera work hard?').

example.q: Think it through: Change to the simple past: 'Meera waters the tree and Kabir buys a powder.'
steps: 'waters' is regular, so add -ed: watered.
'buys' is irregular: buy → bought.
Put the sentence together.
example.answer: Meera watered the tree and Kabir bought a powder.

learn.reallife: When you tell your family what happened at school today, you naturally use the past tense: 'We played kho-kho.'

items.text: Yesterday Ravi ___ his grandmother in Jaipur.
Meera did not ___ the magic powder.
Last Diwali, we ___ diyas on the balcony.
___ you finish your homework last night?
The tree ___ sweet mangoes two summers later.

quiz.q: What is the simple past of 'carry'?
quiz.explain: For verbs ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: carry → carried.
quiz.mistake: Adds -ed without changing y to i

quiz.q: What is the simple past of 'buy'?
quiz.explain: 'Buy' is irregular: buy → bought. 'Brought' is the past of 'bring'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'bought' (buy) and 'brought' (bring)

quiz.q: Which negative sentence in the past tense is correct?
options: She did not took the shortcut.
She did not take the shortcut.
She did not taken the shortcut.
quiz.explain: After 'did not' we use the base verb: did not take.
quiz.mistake: Uses the past form after 'did'

quiz.q: Which verb is irregular?
quiz.explain: 'Go' becomes 'went'; the others just add -ed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every verb adds -ed in the past

quiz.q: Fill in: Last year, our class ___ a trip to the zoo.
quiz.explain: 'Last year' tells us the action is in the past, so we use 'made'.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the time clue 'last year'

quiz.q: Change to a question: 'Kabir sold the powder.'
quiz.explain: Questions in the simple past use 'Did' + subject + base verb.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the past form 'sold' after 'Did'

quiz.q: What is the simple past of 'stop'?
quiz.explain: Short verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: stop → stopped.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

quiz.q: Which time word tells you to use the simple past?
quiz.explain: 'Yesterday' points to the past. 'Tomorrow' and 'next week' are future; 'every day' is a habit.
quiz.mistake: Does not use time words as tense clues

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'I want to tell you what I did yesterday, but I keep saying I fly and I eat! How do I talk about the past?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Yesterday I flew, I ate and I learned the past tense!
teach.nudge: What about verbs like 'go' that don't just add -ed?

learn.hook: What happens when an old animal story learns to rhyme? It becomes a fable in verse!
points: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable told as a poem: a clever fox tricks a bird by praising it.
A fable is a short story, often with animals that talk, which teaches a moral (a lesson).
'In verse' means written in lines of poetry, often with rhythm and rhyme, instead of ordinary paragraphs (prose).
A group of lines in a poem is called a stanza. Words that end with the same sound, like 'tight' and 'delight', are rhyming words.
Many famous fables come from Aesop (ancient Greece) and from the Panchatantra (ancient India).

example.q: Read this original poem: A myna sat upon a tree, / A roti in her beak held tight. / A jackal called, "O bird so fair, / Your song must be a pure delight!" / She sang out loud — the roti fell; / He grabbed it quick and ran from sight. / Now Myna knows that honeyed words / Can hide a plan that isn't right. Which words rhyme, and what is the moral?
steps: Look at the last word of each line: tree, tight, fair, delight, fell, sight, words, right.
'tight', 'delight', 'sight' and 'right' all end with the same '-ight' sound.
The myna lost her roti because she believed the jackal's sweet words.
So the lesson is about not trusting flattery.
example.answer: Rhyming words: tight, delight, sight, right. Moral: don't be fooled by sweet words of flattery.

learn.reallife: Panchatantra tales, Jataka tales and cartoon fables on TV all teach a moral through animal characters.

quiz.q: What is a fable?
options: A true report about a famous person
A long poem about the sea
A short story, often with talking animals, that teaches a moral
quiz.explain: Fables are short stories, usually with animal characters, that end with a lesson.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a fable with a biography or a report

quiz.q: 'The Raven and the Fox' is a fable 'in verse'. What does 'in verse' mean?
quiz.explain: Verse means poetry: lines with rhythm, often with rhyme.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the difference between verse and prose

quiz.q: In the poem, which word rhymes with 'tight'?
quiz.explain: 'Tight' and 'delight' both end with the '-ight' sound.
quiz.mistake: Looks at spelling or meaning instead of the ending sound

quiz.q: In the poem, the jackal said, "O bird so fair, your song must be a pure delight!" Why did he say this?
options: To make the myna open her beak and drop the roti
To make friends with the myna
quiz.explain: He wanted the roti, so he praised her to make her sing and drop it.
quiz.mistake: Believes the jackal's words were honest praise

quiz.q: In the poem, what happened when the myna sang out loud?
options: She flew away with the roti
The roti fell and the jackal grabbed it
quiz.explain: Opening her beak to sing made the roti fall, and the jackal ran off with it.
quiz.mistake: Does not follow the sequence of events in the poem

quiz.q: What is the moral of the myna-and-jackal poem?
options: Do not be fooled by sweet words of flattery
quiz.explain: The myna lost her food because she trusted the jackal's honeyed words.
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail of the story instead of its lesson

quiz.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a:
quiz.explain: Poems are divided into stanzas, just as prose is divided into paragraphs.
quiz.mistake: Uses the prose word 'paragraph' for poetry

quiz.q: Which ancient Indian collection is famous for animal fables?
quiz.explain: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of animal fables with morals.
quiz.mistake: Does not know any traditional source of fables

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My teacher says this poem is a fable in verse. What is a fable, and what does in verse mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! A fable is a lesson-story, and verse means it's a poem. Rhyme time!
teach.nudge: And what do we learn at the end of a fable?

topics.title: Flattery: sweet words with a hidden plan

learn.hook: If someone suddenly says you're the best singer in the whole universe, should you smile — or check your tiffin?
points: Flattery is praise that is too much and not sincere, usually given to get something from the person.
Honest praise is true and fair: 'Your drawing has lovely colours.' Flattery is over the top: 'You are the greatest artist who ever lived!'
Word family: flatter (verb), flattery (noun), flatterer (a person who flatters).
'Honeyed words' and 'sweet talk' are phrases for pleasant words that may hide a trick. The idiom 'to butter someone up' (in Hindi, 'makkhan lagana') means to flatter them.
A wise person enjoys kind words but still thinks: 'Is this true? Why is this person saying it?'

example.q: Think it through: Raju tells Aman, 'You're the smartest boy in the whole world! Can I copy your homework?' Is this honest praise or flattery?
steps: The praise is far too big to be true.
Raju wants something right after praising: to copy homework.
Too-big praise + a hidden purpose = flattery.
example.answer: It is flattery, because the praise is exaggerated and is used to get something.

learn.reallife: Advertisements and some online messages flatter you ('Lucky winner! You are special!') to make you click or buy — so think before you trust.

quiz.explain: It is true, fair and asks for nothing in return.

quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally

quiz.q: 'Stop buttering me up!' What does 'buttering up' mean here?

quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What is the best thing to do when someone flatters you?

Enjoy kind words but think about why they are said
quiz.explain: A wise person stays polite but thinks about the purpose behind the praise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks flattery must be either believed fully or met with anger

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'sincere'?
quiz.explain: The opposite of 'sincere' is 'insincere', formed with the prefix 'in-'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'un-' or 'dis-' without checking the real word

quiz.explain: Flatterers use praise as a tool to get something, like the jackal and the roti.

teach.ask: Gappu is excited: 'Someone told me I'm the most beautiful bird in the galaxy! Then he asked for my seeds. What just happened?'
teach.praise: Tweet! That was flattery — too-sweet praise used as a trick. My seeds are staying with me!
teach.nudge: But why do you think he praised me so much just before asking for my seeds?

learn.hook: The jackal didn't just say 'nice bird' — he piled on adjectives! Let's learn how to compare with them.
points: An adjective describes a noun: a clever jackal, a hungry myna, a tall tree.
Adjectives have three degrees: positive (sweet), comparative (sweeter) and superlative (sweetest).
Use the comparative (+ 'than') for two things: 'The fox is cleverer than the raven.' Use the superlative (+ 'the') for three or more: 'the tallest tree'.
Short adjectives add -er/-est (tall, taller, tallest); long ones use more/most (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful).
Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; many, more, most.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'Of all the birds in the garden, the peacock is the ___ (colourful).'
steps: 'Of all the birds' compares more than two, so we need the superlative.
'Colourful' is a long adjective, so it uses 'most'.
Superlatives take 'the' before them.
example.answer: the most colourful

learn.reallife: Shopping and sports talk is full of comparisons: 'This mango is sweeter', 'Rohit is the fastest runner in our class.'

items.text: An elephant is ___ than a horse.

quiz.q: Which word is an adjective in: 'The hungry myna sat on a branch'?
quiz.explain: 'Hungry' describes the myna, so it is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the noun or verb with the describing word

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i

quiz.q: What is the superlative degree of 'good'?
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good, better, best.
quiz.mistake: Treats an irregular adjective as regular

quiz.q: Which comparison of two people is correct?
options: Rani is taller than her brother.
Rani is tallest than her brother.
Rani is more taller than her brother.
Rani is tall than her brother.
quiz.explain: Comparing two people needs the comparative form 'taller' with 'than'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the superlative or a double comparative for two things

quiz.q: Fill in: 'The Ganga is one of the ___ rivers in India.'
quiz.explain: 'One of the ...' is followed by a superlative: one of the longest rivers.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative after 'one of the'

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'beautiful'?
quiz.explain: Long adjectives use 'more' for the comparative.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to a long adjective

quiz.q: What is the comparative of 'bad'?
quiz.explain: 'Bad' is irregular: bad, worse, worst.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up worse (comparative) and worst (superlative)

quiz.q: What is the superlative of 'big'?
quiz.explain: Short adjectives ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → biggest.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I say my nest is better than my cousin's and the best in the whole tree?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Better for two, best for all. My nest is the cosiest!
teach.nudge: And when I compare my nest with ALL the nests in the tree, which form do I use?

learn.hook: A monkey, a pair of spectacles and one smart girl — what could go wrong? (Everything, and then everything goes right!)
points: 'Rama to the Rescue' is a humorous folk tale in which quick thinking saves the day.
A folk tale is a traditional story passed down by people telling it aloud, often from grandparents to children.
Humour comes from funny situations, surprising twists, silly characters and sound words like 'Plop!'
Words that imitate sounds (plop, buzz, splash, crash) are called onomatopoeia.
When reading, notice the problem, the turning point (where things change) and how the problem is solved.

example.q: Read: At a busy railway station, a cheeky monkey snatched Dadaji's spectacles and leapt onto the roof of a tea stall. People shouted and waved, but the monkey only chattered. Little Lata stayed calm. She held up a banana. Plop! The monkey dropped the spectacles into Dadaji's lap and grabbed the fruit. Everyone laughed and clapped. What was the problem, and how was it solved?
steps: Problem: the monkey took Dadaji's spectacles.
Shouting and waving did not help.
Turning point: Lata calmly held up a banana.
Solution: the monkey dropped the spectacles to grab the fruit.
example.answer: The monkey stole Dadaji's spectacles; Lata got them back by offering it a banana.

learn.reallife: Monkeys at temples and stations in many Indian towns really do snatch things — and people often trade fruit to get them back!

games.title: What happened first?
games.prompt: Put the monkey story in order

The monkey dropped the spectacles and took the fruit.

quiz.q: In the monkey story, what did the monkey snatch?
quiz.explain: The first line says the monkey snatched Dadaji's spectacles.
quiz.mistake: Confuses what was stolen with what was offered

quiz.q: In the story, "People shouted and waved, but the monkey only chattered." What does this show?
options: Shouting did not solve the problem
The monkey gave back the spectacles
quiz.explain: The monkey just chattered and did not return the spectacles, so shouting failed.
quiz.mistake: Assumes noise must have worked

quiz.q: How did Lata get the spectacles back?
options: She held up a banana for the monkey
quiz.explain: The monkey dropped the spectacles to grab the banana Lata held up.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the turning point carefully

quiz.q: Which word in the story is an example of onomatopoeia (a sound word)?
quiz.explain: 'Plop' imitates the sound of the spectacles dropping.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that onomatopoeia means a word that copies a sound

quiz.q: What makes the monkey story humorous?
options: A cheeky monkey and a funny swap of spectacles for a banana
quiz.explain: The silly monkey and the surprising swap make readers laugh.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise what creates humour in a story

quiz.q: What is a folk tale?
options: A news report in a paper
A traditional story passed on by people telling it
quiz.explain: Folk tales are old stories handed down by word of mouth.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a folk tale with factual writing

quiz.q: In the story, 'cheeky' monkey means the monkey was:
quiz.explain: A cheeky person or animal is playfully naughty and bold.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the word 'cheek' (part of the face)

quiz.q: How did the people feel at the end of the story?
quiz.explain: The story ends with 'Everyone laughed and clapped', which shows they were happy and amused.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the last line as a clue to feelings

teach.ask: Gappu giggles: 'Why do people call some stories funny folk tales? What makes them funny?'
teach.praise: Hee-hee-tweet! Old stories passed down, with silly twists — I love folk tales!
teach.nudge: And what makes a folk tale make us laugh?

learn.hook: When something goes wrong, do you panic like a pressure cooker or think like a detective?
points: Presence of mind means staying calm and thinking quickly in a sudden or difficult situation.
A person with presence of mind is quick-witted, calm and resourceful (good at finding ways to solve problems).
Useful phrases: 'keep a cool head' (stay calm), 'think on your feet' (think quickly), 'at one's wits' end' (not knowing what to do).
Panic usually makes problems worse; a calm, clever idea often fixes them.
In an emergency, presence of mind also means telling a trusted adult quickly or calling helplines like 112.

example.q: Think it through: During a class picnic, the bus driver says the road ahead is blocked. Students start crying. Priya asks, 'Is there another road? Can we inform our teacher and parents?' What does Priya show?
steps: Others panic and cry.
Priya stays calm.
She thinks of a practical solution and informs adults.
Calm + quick thinking = presence of mind.
example.answer: Priya shows presence of mind: she stays calm and thinks of sensible next steps.

learn.reallife: Firefighters, doctors in emergency rooms and even goalkeepers need presence of mind every day.

games.title: Presence of mind: true or false?

quiz.q: What does 'presence of mind' mean?
options: Being present in class every day
Staying calm and thinking quickly in a sudden situation
quiz.explain: Presence of mind is about calm, quick thinking when something unexpected happens.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'presence' to mean attendance

quiz.q: In the monkey story, Lata 'stayed calm' and held up a banana. Which quality did she show?
quiz.explain: She stayed calm and found a quick, clever solution.
quiz.mistake: Does not link calm thinking with presence of mind

quiz.q: What does 'quick-witted' mean?
options: able to think fast and cleverly
quiz.explain: 'Wits' means the mind's cleverness, so quick-witted = fast, clever thinking.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'quick' to be about physical speed

quiz.q: 'When the lights went out on stage, Arun kept a cool head and switched on his torch.' 'Kept a cool head' means he:
quiz.explain: To keep a cool head is an idiom for staying calm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'calm'?
quiz.explain: 'Calm' means peaceful and relaxed; 'nervous' is its opposite.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a synonym instead of an antonym

quiz.q: A 'resourceful' person is someone who:
options: finds clever ways to solve problems
quiz.explain: Resourceful means good at finding solutions, especially in difficult situations.
quiz.mistake: Thinks resourceful means rich

quiz.q: Your friend's kite string gets stuck on an electric wire. What shows presence of mind?
options: Climb the pole to get it
Leave it and tell an adult; never pull it from the wire
quiz.explain: Electric wires are dangerous; the calm and safe choice is to leave it and inform an adult.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being brave means taking dangerous risks

quiz.q: 'Meena was at her wits' end when she lost her ticket.' This means Meena:
options: did not know what to do
was at the end of the road
quiz.explain: Being at your wits' end means you are so worried you don't know what to do.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: 'Grown-ups keep saying someone has presence of mind. Does that mean they came to school?'
teach.praise: Tweet! It means staying calm and thinking fast when trouble comes. I'll keep a cool beak!
teach.nudge: But what should a person do in a sudden problem — panic, or something else?

learn.hook: Punctuation marks are the traffic signals of writing — they tell readers when to stop, pause, ask or shout!
points: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), question mark (?) or exclamation mark (!).
Speech marks (quotation marks " ") go around the exact words someone says: Lata said, "Wait, I have an idea."
Put a comma after 'said' before the spoken words, and keep the end punctuation of the speech inside the closing speech marks.
Commas separate items in a list: bananas, apples and guavas. An apostrophe shows possession (Dadaji's spectacles) or missing letters (don't = do not).
Proper nouns like names of people, places and days always begin with a capital letter: Lata, Jaipur, Monday.

example.q: Think it through: Punctuate this: lata said dont worry dadaji
steps: Start with a capital: Lata.
Add a comma after 'said'.
Open speech marks and use a capital letter for the first spoken word: "Don't...
'dont' needs an apostrophe: don't.
Dadaji is a name, so capital D, and close with a full stop inside the speech marks.
example.answer: Lata said, "Don't worry, Dadaji."

learn.reallife: Chat messages, posters and signboards all need correct punctuation — 'Let's eat, Grandma!' is very different from 'Let's eat Grandma!'

items.text: "Where are my spectacles___ asked Dadaji.
What a cheeky monkey___

Lata___s quick idea saved the day.

quiz.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Lata said, I have a banana.
quiz.explain: It has a comma after 'said', speech marks, a capital 'I' and the full stop inside the closing mark.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out speech marks or capital letters

quiz.q: Which mark ends a question?
quiz.explain: Questions end with a question mark (?).
quiz.mistake: Ends every sentence with a full stop

quiz.q: In 'Dadaji's spectacles', the apostrophe shows:
options: that the spectacles belong to Dadaji
quiz.explain: Here 's shows possession: the spectacles belong to Dadaji.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an apostrophe always means a missing letter

quiz.q: What is the short form of 'do not'?
quiz.explain: The apostrophe takes the place of the missing 'o': don't.
quiz.mistake: Puts the apostrophe in the wrong place

quiz.q: Which word must always start with a capital letter?
quiz.explain: Jaipur is the name of a place, a proper noun, so it takes a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Does not know proper nouns need capitals

quiz.q: Which mark fits best? "Oh no___" cried Dadaji when the monkey took his glasses.
quiz.explain: 'Oh no' shows a strong feeling, so it takes an exclamation mark.
quiz.mistake: Uses a question mark for a strong feeling

quiz.q: Where do speech marks go?
options: Around the exact words a person says
At the start of each paragraph only
Around the name of the speaker
quiz.explain: Speech marks enclose only the words actually spoken.
quiz.mistake: Puts the speaker's name inside the speech marks

quiz.q: Which list is punctuated correctly?
options: I packed a torch, a map and a water bottle.
I packed, a torch a map and a water bottle.
I packed a torch a map, and, a water bottle.
I packed a torch. a map and a water bottle.
quiz.explain: Commas separate items in a list, and 'and' joins the last two.
quiz.mistake: Places commas randomly

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'When I write what Lata said, where do all those little marks go?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Speech marks around the spoken words, a comma after said and a capital to start. Perfect!
teach.nudge: And what goes around the exact words someone says?

learn.hook: A noisy cricket fan and a quiet painter — can they be best friends? Let's read and see!
points: 'The Unlikely Best Friends' is about a friendship between two people who seem very different.
'Unlikely' means not expected. An unlikely friendship is one people would not expect.
Good friends can have different hobbies, habits and backgrounds; what matters is respect, trust and care.
Characters change in a story. Notice how their feelings at the start differ from their feelings at the end.
Look for clues in what characters say and do to understand their nature (character traits).

example.q: Read: Tara loved noisy cricket matches. Bholu, her new neighbour, loved quiet painting. "We have nothing in common," Tara grumbled. Then Tara hurt her ankle and had to sit at home for a week. Bholu came over with his paints and taught her to paint the sunset. On Sports Day, when Bholu was nervous before his race, Tara cheered louder than anyone. How did Tara's feelings about Bholu change?
steps: At first Tara said, 'We have nothing in common.'
When she was hurt, Bholu helped her by teaching her to paint.
Later, Tara cheered loudly for Bholu at Sports Day.
So she went from thinking they were too different to being his supportive friend.
example.answer: At first she thought they had nothing in common, but after Bholu helped her, she became his caring friend.

learn.reallife: Your best friend may love maths while you love music — differences can make a friendship more fun.

games.title: Tara and Bholu

The passage calls him her new neighbour.
She had to sit at home for a week.
Bholu taught Tara to play cricket.

quiz.q: In the story, Tara loved noisy cricket matches and Bholu loved quiet painting. Why is their friendship 'unlikely'?
quiz.explain: 'Unlikely' means not expected; their very different hobbies make the friendship surprising.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'unlikely'

quiz.q: What did Tara say at first about Bholu?
quiz.explain: Early in the story Tara grumbled, 'We have nothing in common.'
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the beginning and the end of the story

quiz.q: Tara "grumbled" when she said they had nothing in common. 'Grumbled' means she spoke:

quiz.mistake: Guesses the meaning without using the context

quiz.explain: Bholu came over with his paints and taught her to paint.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the detail in the passage

quiz.q: Why did Tara cheer louder than anyone on Sports Day?
options: She wanted to win a prize
Bholu was nervous and she wanted to support him
quiz.explain: The passage says Bholu was nervous before his race, so Tara supported him.

quiz.q: Which word best describes Bholu when he visited Tara?
quiz.explain: Visiting a hurt friend and teaching her something new shows that he cares.
quiz.mistake: Does not judge character from actions

quiz.q: What is the main idea of Tara and Bholu's story?
options: Friends can be different and still care for each other
quiz.explain: The story shows two very different children becoming caring friends.
quiz.mistake: Picks a small detail instead of the main idea

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'unlikely'?
quiz.explain: Removing the prefix 'un-' gives 'likely', the opposite.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'unlikely' with 'unlike'

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'I'm a bird and my friend is a squirrel. We're so different. Can we really be best friends?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Different feathers, same kind heart. Squirrel and I will be best friends forever!
teach.nudge: But what really matters in a friendship, if not being the same?

learn.hook: Some of the best stories are tiny true-life moments — just a few lines that show who a person really was.
points: An anecdote is a short, interesting story about a real person or a real event.
Anecdotes are usually told in the past tense and often show a person's character: their wit, kindness or courage.
Many anecdotes are told about Emperor Akbar and Birbal, a witty member of his court. These stories have been told and retold for centuries as popular folk tales.
An anecdote has a setting, a small problem or question, and a clever or surprising ending.
A friendship can be 'unlikely' when two people are very different in age, position or nature, yet value each other.

example.q: Read this anecdote, told in our own words: One day Akbar drew a line on the floor and said, 'Make this line shorter without rubbing out any part of it.' The courtiers were puzzled. Birbal simply drew a longer line beside it. Now Akbar's line looked shorter! What does this anecdote show about Birbal?
steps: The problem: shorten a line without touching it.
Others could not think of a way.
Birbal changed the comparison by drawing a longer line next to it.
This shows quick, clever thinking.
example.answer: It shows that Birbal was witty and could think in a clever, unusual way.

learn.reallife: Your grandparents' stories about 'the day the first TV came to our street' are family anecdotes!

games.title: Anecdote or not?
items: a short, funny true story about your grandfather as a boy
a brief story about how a famous scientist solved a puzzle
a little story about what happened at your cousin's wedding

games.title: Line puzzle sequence

He asked the courtiers to make it shorter without rubbing it out.
Birbal drew a longer line beside it.

quiz.q: What is an anecdote?
options: A short, interesting story about a real person or event
quiz.explain: An anecdote is brief and about something that really happened (or is told as if it did).
quiz.mistake: Confuses an anecdote with any kind of long story

quiz.q: Anecdotes are usually told in which tense?
quiz.explain: They describe something that already happened, so they use the past tense.
quiz.mistake: Does not link storytelling with the past tense

quiz.q: In the anecdote, Akbar asked his courtiers to make his line shorter. What was the tricky condition?
options: They had to use red ink
They could not rub out any part of it
They had to close their eyes
quiz.explain: The challenge was to shorten the line without erasing any part of it.
quiz.mistake: Misses the key condition in the problem

quiz.q: How did Birbal solve the line puzzle?
options: He drew a longer line beside it
He rubbed out half the line
He covered it with a cloth
quiz.explain: Next to a longer line, Akbar's line looked shorter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks he must have erased part of the line

quiz.q: In the anecdote, "The courtiers were puzzled." 'Puzzled' means:
quiz.explain: To be puzzled is to be confused and unable to understand something.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the word 'puzzle' (a game) without context

quiz.q: Which quality does the line anecdote show in Birbal?
quiz.explain: Wit means quick, clever thinking — exactly what Birbal showed.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the action with a character trait

quiz.q: Who were Akbar's 'courtiers'?
options: people who attended the emperor at his court
quiz.explain: A court is where a king or emperor met people; courtiers were the people there.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a royal court with a sports court

quiz.q: Why might the friendship of an emperor and a courtier be called 'unlikely'?
options: They were very different in position and power
They spoke to each other only by letters
quiz.explain: An emperor and a member of his court were very different in rank, so a close friendship would be surprising.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the difference in position

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My teacher told an anecdote today. Is that a kind of dinosaur?'
teach.praise: Chirp! An anecdote is a short, true-life story that shows what a person is like. No dinosaurs!
teach.nudge: Is an anecdote made up, or is it about a real person?

learn.hook: Friendship, Birbal, team, palace — all nouns! But each one is a different kind. Let's sort them.
points: A noun names a person, place, animal, thing or idea.
Common nouns are general names (girl, city, river). Proper nouns are particular names and begin with capitals (Tara, Agra, Yamuna).
Collective nouns name a group as one: a team of players, a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a swarm of bees, a bunch of grapes.
Abstract nouns name feelings, qualities or ideas we cannot see or touch: friendship, kindness, courage, honesty, wisdom.
Many abstract nouns are made with suffixes: friend → friendship, kind → kindness, brave → bravery, wise → wisdom.

example.q: Think it through: Find the kinds of nouns in: 'Birbal's wisdom amazed the crowd in Agra.'
steps: Birbal and Agra are particular names → proper nouns.
Wisdom is an idea we can't touch → abstract noun.
Crowd names a group of people → collective noun.
example.answer: Proper: Birbal, Agra; abstract: wisdom; collective: crowd.

learn.reallife: Your school (proper noun), your class team (collective noun) and your friendship (abstract noun) are all around you!

quiz.q: Which is a proper noun?
quiz.explain: Agra names one particular city, so it is a proper noun.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any place word is a proper noun

quiz.q: Which is an abstract noun?
quiz.explain: Friendship is a feeling or relationship we cannot touch.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'friend' (a person) with 'friendship' (an idea)

quiz.q: Fill in the collective noun: a ___ of bees.
quiz.explain: Bees fly in a swarm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the collective noun for a different group

quiz.q: Which is the abstract noun formed from 'brave'?
quiz.explain: Adding -ry gives the noun 'bravery'. 'Bravely' is an adverb.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the adverb with the noun

quiz.q: In 'The team won the match', what kind of noun is 'team'?
quiz.explain: 'Team' names a group of players as one unit.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise a group word

quiz.q: Which words need capital letters in: 'we visited the taj mahal in agra'?
quiz.explain: Proper nouns (Taj Mahal, Agra) and the first word of a sentence take capitals.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that proper nouns need capitals

quiz.q: What is the abstract noun formed from 'wise'?
quiz.explain: 'Wise' becomes 'wisdom'. 'Wisely' is an adverb and 'wiser' is a comparative.
quiz.mistake: Adds -ness to every adjective

quiz.q: Which is a common noun?
quiz.explain: 'Girl' is a general name; the others are particular names (proper nouns).
quiz.mistake: Confuses common and proper nouns

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'I know nouns are naming words. But my teacher says friendship is a noun too. I can't even see it!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Some nouns name things we can see, and abstract nouns name ideas like friendship. I get it!
teach.nudge: Which kind of noun names something we cannot see or touch, like friendship?

learn.hook: If you could write a wish for the kind of friend you want to be, what would it say?
points: 'A Friend's Prayer' is a poem in which the speaker wishes to be a good, true friend.
A prayer is a humble wish or request. Lines starting with 'Let me be...' express such wishes.
The rhyme scheme shows which lines rhyme. We give the same letter to lines that rhyme: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme.
The speaker of a poem is the voice saying the words (often 'I' or 'me').
Poets use repetition (repeating words like 'Let me be') to make an idea stronger and give the poem a rhythm.
The poem's second stanza (also original): 'Let me be kind when you are wrong, / And help you up and make you strong; / For friendship isn't gold or gift — / It's a hand held out, a heart to lift.'

example.q: Read this original stanza: Let me be the friend who listens well, / Who keeps the secrets you choose to tell, / Who shares an umbrella when rain falls down, / And gently turns away your frown. What is its rhyme scheme?
steps: Last words: well, tell, down, frown.
'well' and 'tell' rhyme → A A.
'down' and 'frown' rhyme → B B.
example.answer: AABB

learn.reallife: Friendship bands on Friendship Day, birthday cards and school farewell speeches often use short rhyming poems like this.

quiz.explain: Line 3 says the friend shares an umbrella when rain falls down.

quiz.explain: Keeping a friend's secrets shows you can be trusted.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the action with the quality

quiz.q: The poem's second stanza: "Let me be kind when you are wrong, / And help you up and make you strong; / For friendship isn't gold or gift — / It's a hand held out, a heart to lift." According to it, what is friendship?
options: A hand held out and a heart to lift
quiz.explain: The last line says friendship is 'a hand held out, a heart to lift'.
quiz.mistake: Picks the idea the poem rejects

quiz.q: In the poem, "Let me be kind when you are wrong." What does the speaker promise?
options: To be gentle even when the friend makes a mistake
To laugh at the friend's mistakes
To leave when the friend is wrong
quiz.explain: Being kind when someone is wrong means being gentle and forgiving.
quiz.mistake: Thinks friends should be kind only when things are fine

quiz.q: Which word in the poem rhymes with 'wrong'?
quiz.explain: 'Wrong' and 'strong' share the '-ong' sound.
quiz.mistake: Does not compare ending sounds

quiz.q: Why is the poem called a 'prayer'?
options: It is sung in a temple only
It is a humble wish to be a good friend
It is a story about a king
quiz.explain: A prayer is a heartfelt wish or request; the poem wishes 'Let me be...' a good friend.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a prayer must be linked to one particular place

quiz.q: What is the rhyme scheme of a stanza where lines 1 and 2 rhyme, and lines 3 and 4 rhyme?
quiz.explain: Matching letters show rhyming lines: first pair A A, second pair B B.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how rhyme schemes are labelled

quiz.q: Repeating 'Let me be' at the start of both stanzas is an example of:
quiz.explain: Using the same words again for effect is repetition.
quiz.mistake: Confuses repetition with rhyme

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'My teacher said this poem has an AABB rhyme scheme. What does that alphabet soup mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! AABB means the first two lines rhyme and the next two rhyme. Well, tell, down, frown!
teach.nudge: Which lines rhyme with each other in AABB?

learn.hook: Add three little letters to 'kind' and you get 'kindness' — a word that can change someone's whole day!
points: Kindness means being friendly, caring and helpful to others, without expecting anything back.
The suffix -ness turns adjectives into nouns: kind → kindness, happy → happiness, sad → sadness.
The suffix -ful means 'full of': care → careful, help → helpful, thank → thankful. The suffix -less means 'without': care → careless, help → helpless.
The prefix un- means 'not': kind → unkind, fair → unfair, friendly → unfriendly.
Small acts of kindness: sharing, listening, including a new student, saying 'thank you' and 'sorry'.

example.q: Think it through: Make two new words from 'help', one meaning 'full of help' and one meaning 'without help'.
steps: -ful means 'full of' → helpful.
-less means 'without' → helpless.
example.answer: helpful and helpless

learn.reallife: Helping a younger child find their classroom, or inviting a new student to sit with you at lunch, are everyday acts of kindness.

games.title: Kind or unkind?

inviting a new student to play
saying thank you to the bus driver

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'kind'?
quiz.explain: Adding -ness to the adjective 'kind' makes the noun 'kindness'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the adverb or comparative with the noun

quiz.q: The suffix '-less' means:
quiz.explain: -less means without: careless = without care.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up -less and -ful

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'careful'?
quiz.explain: Careful (full of care) and careless (without care) are opposites.
quiz.mistake: Adds un- instead of changing the suffix

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'friendly'?
quiz.explain: The prefix un- means 'not': unfriendly. 'Friendless' means having no friends.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'unfriendly' with 'friendless'

quiz.q: Which is an act of kindness?
options: Keeping the umbrella only for yourself
Splashing a friend with puddle water
Sharing your umbrella with a friend in the rain
quiz.explain: Sharing to help someone is kind.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise a caring action

quiz.q: Fill in: Mohan was ___ to the old man and helped him cross the road.
quiz.explain: After 'was' we need an adjective; helping the old man shows he was kind.
quiz.mistake: Uses the noun where an adjective is needed

quiz.q: What does 'thankful' mean?
quiz.explain: -ful means 'full of', so thankful means full of thanks.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of -ful

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: Change y to i and add -ness: happiness.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i before -ness

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did the word kind grow into kindness and unkind? Are words magic?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Prefixes go at the front, suffixes at the end, and they make new words. Word magic!
teach.nudge: What do we add at the end of a word to make kind into kindness?

learn.hook: Imagine saying 'Tara said Tara will lend Tara's book to Tara's friend.' Pronouns save us from that tongue-twister!
points: A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun: Tara → she, the book → it, Tara and I → we.
Subject pronouns do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns receive the action: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs ('This pencil is mine').
Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves ('She taught herself to paint').
Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: 'yours', not 'your's'; 'its' (belonging to it) is different from 'it's' (it is).

example.q: Think it through: Replace the repeated nouns: 'Arjun lost Arjun's bag, so Priya helped Arjun find the bag.'
steps: 'Arjun's' → his.
Second 'Arjun' (object of 'helped') → him.
'the bag' → it.
example.answer: Arjun lost his bag, so Priya helped him find it.

learn.reallife: Whenever you chat with friends — 'Is this yours?' 'No, it's mine!' — you're using pronouns.

items.text: Riya and ___ went to the market.

This tiffin box is not yours; it is ___.
The children made the rangoli by ___.
The dog wagged ___ tail.

quiz.q: Which word is a pronoun?
quiz.explain: 'They' replaces a plural noun, so it is a pronoun.
quiz.mistake: Confuses pronouns with other parts of speech

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the subject pronoun correctly?
options: Tara and me painted the sunset.
Me and Tara painted the sunset.
Tara and I painted the sunset.
Tara and myself painted the sunset.
quiz.explain: The subject of the sentence needs the subject pronoun 'I'.

quiz.q: Fill in: Mother gave ___ a hug.
quiz.explain: 'Us' is the object pronoun that receives the hug.
quiz.mistake: Uses a subject pronoun after a verb

quiz.q: Which is a reflexive pronoun?
quiz.explain: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves.
quiz.mistake: Confuses object or possessive forms with reflexive ones

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Is this umbrella ___?'
quiz.explain: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: yours.
quiz.mistake: Adds an apostrophe to a possessive pronoun

quiz.q: Which sentence uses 'its' correctly?
quiz.explain: 'Its' shows belonging; 'it's' means 'it is'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'its' with 'it's'

quiz.q: Replace the noun: 'Meena and Raju are friends. Meena and Raju study together.'
quiz.explain: Meena and Raju (subject, more than one person) → they.
quiz.mistake: Uses an object or reflexive pronoun as the subject

quiz.q: Fill in: 'The friends made a promise to ___ to be kind.'
quiz.explain: The correct reflexive form for 'the friends' is 'themselves'.
quiz.mistake: Uses an incorrect form like 'theirselves'

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'Why do we say she and her instead of using names every time?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Pronouns stand in place of nouns so we don't repeat names again and again. I like it!
teach.nudge: What does a pronoun do to a noun in a sentence?

topics.title: A story told by a chair

learn.hook: What if the chair you're sitting on could talk? What stories would it tell about you?
points: 'The Chair' is a story that centres on an ordinary chair and the feelings and imagination around it.
When a non-living thing is given human feelings or actions, it is called personification ('the chair felt young again').
A story told by 'I' is in the first person. The narrator here is the chair itself.
The setting is where and when a story happens; the characters are the people, animals or things in it.
Readers can infer (work out) feelings from clues, even when the feeling is not named.

example.q: Read: I am an old wooden chair on Nani's verandah. For forty years I have held tired visitors, giggling grandchildren and one very fat cat. My legs creak now, and yesterday someone said, "Let's throw it away." But little Chintu painted my arms blue and said, "You're my throne!" I felt young again. How does the chair feel at the start and at the end?
steps: 'My legs creak now' and 'Let's throw it away' suggest the chair feels old and unwanted.

learn.hook: A blanket can be a tent, a broom can be a horse, and a chair can be a throne — all you need is imagination!
points: Imagination is the power to form pictures and ideas in your mind of things that are not really present.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when) and a plot (what happens, with a problem and an ending).
Writers often start with a 'What if...?' question: What if my school bag could fly?
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginative (adjective), imaginary (adjective: not real).
'Imaginative' describes a creative person or idea; 'imaginary' describes something that exists only in the mind.

example.q: Think it through: Ananya writes: 'What if the old chair could walk at night?' Name the parts she needs to build a story.
steps: Character: the old chair (and maybe the family).
Setting: the house, at night.
Plot: a problem (the chair wants to explore) and an ending (it returns before morning).
example.answer: She needs characters, a setting and a plot with a problem and an ending.

learn.reallife: Cardboard-box rockets, rangoli designs and the games you invent with friends all come from imagination.

learn.hook: Empathy is like trying on someone else's shoes — even a chair's! — to feel what they feel.
points: Empathy means understanding and sharing the feelings of another person (or imagining how a thing or animal might feel).
Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy goes further — you imagine yourself in their place.
Feeling words help us show empathy: lonely, hurt, proud, grateful, nervous, relieved.
Conjunctions are joining words: and (adds), but (contrasts), or (gives a choice), so (shows result), because (gives a reason).
Example: 'The chair felt sad because someone wanted to throw it away, but Chintu loved it.'

example.q: Think it through: Join with the right conjunction: 'Meena's friend was crying. Meena sat beside her and listened.'
steps: The second sentence is the result of the first.

Join them.
example.answer: Meena's friend was crying, so Meena sat beside her and listened.

learn.reallife: When a classmate loses a match or a pet, saying 'I can imagine how hard that is' shows empathy.

topics.title: The neem tree and its uses

learn.hook: Why would anyone brush their teeth with a twig? Meet the neem tree — India's bitter but brilliant friend!
points: 'Neem Baba' is a lesson about the neem tree and the many ways it helps people.
The neem tree (scientific name Azadirachta indica) is native to the Indian subcontinent and grows well in hot, dry places.
Its leaves taste bitter. Traditionally, neem twigs (called 'datun') have been used to clean teeth.
People traditionally keep dried neem leaves with stored grains and woollen clothes to keep insects away. Oil from neem seeds is used in some soaps and natural insect repellents.
A big neem tree gives cool shade, and its small white flowers smell sweet.

example.q: Read: Outside our school stands a huge neem tree. Its bitter leaves rustle in the breeze, and its thick branches give cool shade in May. Grandpa still cleans his teeth with a neem twig. Every year Ma puts dried neem leaves in the rice tin to keep insects away. The children call the tree 'Neem Baba' because it seems wise, old and kind. Give two uses of the neem tree from the passage.
steps: Grandpa cleans his teeth with a neem twig → use 1.
Ma keeps dried neem leaves in the rice tin to keep insects away → use 2.
Its branches give cool shade → use 3.
example.answer: Any two: cleaning teeth with a twig, keeping insects away from rice, giving cool shade.

learn.reallife: You may see neem trees along roads and in school compounds, and neem in soaps and toothpastes on shop shelves.

learn.hook: One tree can give shade to a whole playground for a hundred years. What can one child give back?
points: Conservation means protecting and carefully using nature — trees, water, animals and soil — so that it lasts for the future.
We can help by planting trees, saving water, not wasting paper and following the 3 Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
Van Mahotsav, a tree-planting festival, is celebrated in India in the first week of July. World Environment Day is on 5 June.
In the Chipko movement of the 1970s, villagers in the Himalayan hills hugged trees to stop them from being cut down. ('Chipko' means 'to stick' or 'hug'.)
Compound words join two words to make one: rain + water = rainwater; sun + light = sunlight; wild + life = wildlife.

example.q: Think it through: Sort these actions into Reduce, Reuse or Recycle: carrying a cloth bag instead of taking a new plastic one; using an old jam jar as a pencil holder; sending old newspapers to be made into new paper.
steps: Not taking a new plastic bag means using less → Reduce.
Using the jar again for a new job → Reuse.
Turning old paper into new paper → Recycle.
example.answer: Cloth bag → Reduce; jam jar pencil holder → Reuse; newspapers to make new paper → Recycle.

learn.reallife: Turning off the tap while brushing, carrying a steel water bottle and planting a sapling on your birthday are everyday conservation.

learn.hook: Where is the bird? In the tree, on the branch, among the leaves — prepositions are word maps!
points: A preposition shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word — often place, time or direction.
Place: in (inside), on (touching the surface), under (below), beside (next to), between (two things), among (more than two).
Time: at for exact times (at 7 o'clock), on for days and dates (on Monday, on 5 June), in for months, years and seasons (in July, in 2024, in summer).
Use 'since' for a starting point (since 2015) and 'for' for a length of time (for ten years).
Direction: into, out of, across, through, towards ('The squirrel ran up the trunk').

topics.title: The world through a bird's eyes

learn.hook: Ever wondered what your school looks like to a kite flying overhead? Let's borrow a bird's wings!
points: 'What a Bird Thought' is a poem about how a bird sees and thinks about the world around it.
In a poem, the speaker may be an animal or a thing, not a person. Here the speaker is a bird.
A 'bird's-eye view' means a view from high above, where big things look small.
Poets use images (word pictures) so we can see what the speaker sees.
To understand a poem, read it twice, picture each line, and ask: Who is speaking? What do they see? How do they feel?

example.q: Read this original poem: From high above, the town looks small, / The cars are scattered painted toys; / The river is a silver thread, / The bus, a beetle, makes no noise. / I wonder if the people know / How tiny all their worries seem / When seen from up among the clouds, / Where every road is like a dream. Who is the speaker and what do they notice?
steps: 'From high above' and 'among the clouds' show the speaker is flying — a bird.
The bird sees cars like toys, the river like a thread, the bus like a beetle.
It also wonders whether people know how small their worries look from above.
example.answer: A bird flying high; it notices that everything below looks tiny, and so do people's worries.

topics.title: Seeing from another point of view

learn.hook: To an ant, a puddle is an ocean. To you, it's just a puddle. Who is right? Both!
points: Perspective (point of view) is the way someone sees or thinks about something. It depends on where they are and what they know.
The same event can look different to different people: rain is a joy for a farmer but a problem for a cricket match.
First-person writing uses 'I', 'me', 'we' (the narrator is in the story). Third-person writing uses 'he', 'she', 'they' (the narrator is outside the story).
Changing the point of view can change how a story feels. Imagine your school day told by your school bag!
Seeing other perspectives helps us understand people better and avoid quick judgements.

example.q: Think it through: Rewrite in the first person, as if the bird is speaking: 'The bird looked down and saw the town.'
steps: The narrator becomes the bird itself.
Replace 'The bird' with 'I'.
Keep the rest of the sentence.
example.answer: I looked down and saw the town.

teach.nudge: Why might the ant and I see the same puddle differently?

learn.hook: 'The bus is like a beetle' and 'The bus is a beetle' — one little word makes all the difference!
points: A simile compares two different things using 'like' or 'as': 'The cars look like toys', 'as light as a feather'.
A metaphor compares by saying one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The river is a silver thread.'
Both help readers picture something clearly and in a fresh way.
Common similes: as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as white as snow, as slow as a snail.
Tip: look for 'like' or 'as ... as' to spot a simile; if one thing is simply called another, it is a metaphor.

example.q: Think it through: Is this a simile or a metaphor? 'Grandma's lap is a soft pillow.'
steps: Look for 'like' or 'as' — there isn't one.
It says the lap IS a pillow.
So it is a metaphor.
example.answer: A metaphor.

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators love them: 'He's a wall at the crease!' (metaphor) or 'The ball flew like a rocket!' (simile).

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Simile, metaphor, simile, metaphor... they both compare things. What's the difference?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A simile uses like or as; a metaphor just says it IS the thing. I'm as happy as a lark!
teach.nudge: Which one uses the words 'like' or 'as'?

learn.hook: Your kitchen masala box is a treasure chest — full of colours, smells and centuries of wisdom!
points: 'Spices that Heal Us' is an informative lesson about common Indian spices and how they have traditionally been used for good health.
Turmeric (haldi) is the bright yellow powder made from the underground stem of the turmeric plant. Haldi milk is a popular home drink for colds.
Ginger (adrak) is also an underground stem. Ginger tea is a common home remedy for a sore throat.
Cloves (laung) are dried flower buds, cinnamon (dalchini) is tree bark, and black pepper (kali mirch) is a dried fruit of a climbing vine.
Home remedies can soothe small troubles, but a doctor must treat real illnesses. Never eat spices in large amounts as 'medicine'.

example.q: Read: When Aman caught a cold, Nani made him a cup of warm milk with a pinch of haldi. The next day she brewed ginger tea with tulsi leaves. "These spices have been used in Indian kitchens for centuries," she said. "They add flavour, and many people use them for small troubles like a sore throat. But for a real illness, we always visit the doctor." Name the two drinks Nani made, and what she says about real illness.
steps: Day 1: warm milk with haldi.
Day 2: ginger tea with tulsi leaves.
Her last line: for a real illness, we always visit the doctor.
example.answer: Haldi milk and ginger-tulsi tea; for a real illness, the family visits the doctor.

learn.reallife: Haldi in dal, jeera in rice, elaichi in kheer and ginger in chai — spices are in almost every Indian meal.

teach.praise: Tweet! Spices add flavour and help with small troubles, but for real illness we go to the doctor. Smart!

learn.hook: Your grandparents know things no textbook taught them — like which leaf soothes a cough. That's traditional knowledge!
points: Traditional knowledge is wisdom that people learn by experience and pass down from one generation to the next, often by word of mouth.
In India, knowledge about spices, plants, farming and cooking has been shared within families for centuries.

Spices come from different plant parts: seeds (jeera, ajwain, methi), bark (cinnamon), flower buds (cloves), underground stems (ginger, turmeric), fruits (black pepper), and flower parts (saffron comes from the thread-like parts of a crocus flower).
Kerala is famous for growing spices like black pepper and cardamom; Kashmir is famous for saffron (kesar).
Useful words: generation, heritage, remedy, ancestor, ingredient.

example.q: Think it through: Mira's great-grandmother taught her grandmother, who taught her mother, who taught Mira how to make jeera water. What kind of knowledge is this, and how was it passed on?
steps: It moved from grandparent to parent to child.
It was learnt by practice in the kitchen, not from a textbook.
Knowledge passed down through generations is traditional knowledge.
example.answer: Traditional knowledge, passed down from one generation to the next.

learn.reallife: Grandma's recipe for achaar, the way farmers read the clouds, and Mehendi patterns are all traditional knowledge.

teach.praise: Chirp! Traditional knowledge is passed down by elders, generation to generation. Nani is a walking library!
teach.nudge: Who taught Nani all this, and how did it reach her?

topics.title: A, an, the and much or many

learn.hook: Is it 'a onion' or 'an onion'? 'Much cloves' or 'many cloves'? Let's spice up our grammar!
points: Use 'a' before a consonant SOUND (a clove, a university) and 'an' before a vowel SOUND (an onion, an hour). Listen to the sound, not the letter.
Use 'the' for something specific or already mentioned: 'I bought a lemon. The lemon was juicy.'
Countable nouns can be counted: one clove, two cloves. Uncountable nouns cannot: salt, water, milk, rice, advice.
Use 'many' and 'a few' with countable nouns; 'much' and 'a little' with uncountable nouns.
We count uncountable nouns using measure words: a pinch of salt, a cup of milk, a spoonful of honey.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in: 'Nani added ___ pinch of salt and ___ few cloves, but not ___ ginger.' (choose from a / an / much / many)
steps: 'pinch' starts with a consonant sound → a pinch.
'cloves' are countable → a few cloves.
'ginger' here is uncountable → much ginger.
example.answer: a pinch, a few cloves, not much ginger

learn.reallife: Recipes are full of these: 'a cup of rice', 'an onion', 'a little oil', 'many curry leaves'.

learn.hook: Can you lose a match and still be the hero of the day? This story says yes!
points: 'Change of Heart' is a sports story about how a person's feelings and choices can change.
A 'change of heart' is an idiom meaning a change in one's opinion or feelings, usually towards something kinder.
Sports stories have a goal (winning), a conflict (a tough opponent or a hard choice) and a turning point.
Kabaddi is a team sport from India in which a 'raider' enters the other half and tries to tag opponents while saying 'kabaddi, kabaddi'.
When reading, note how a character's thoughts at the start differ from their actions at the end.

example.q: Read: Sana wanted to win the kabaddi final at any cost. Late in the match, the rival captain, Divya, slipped and twisted her ankle. "Keep going! Now we'll win easily!" shouted Sana's teammates. But when Sana saw Divya wince in pain, she had a change of heart. She stopped, helped Divya up and called for the first-aid kit. Sana's team lost by two points, yet the whole crowd clapped for her. What was Sana's change of heart?
steps: At the start she wanted to win 'at any cost'.
When Divya got hurt, her teammates wanted to keep playing.
Sana saw Divya's pain and stopped to help her.
She chose kindness over winning.
example.answer: She stopped caring only about winning and helped her injured rival instead.

learn.reallife: Some real athletes have stopped to help a fallen rival in races — and crowds remember those moments longer than the results.

learn.hook: The scoreboard shows who won the game. Sportsmanship shows who won respect.
points: Sportsmanship means playing fairly, following the rules, respecting opponents and accepting results gracefully.
A 'good sport' wins without boasting and loses without sulking.
Useful words: fair play, opponent (the person you play against), teammate, referee/umpire, gracious, honour.
Opposites: win ↔ lose, victory ↔ defeat, fair ↔ unfair, teammate ↔ opponent.
Shaking hands after a match, cheering good play by the other side and accepting the umpire's decision are signs of sportsmanship.

example.q: Think it through: In a cricket match, Kiran knows the ball touched his bat before the catch, but the umpire did not see it. He walks off the field anyway. What does this show?
steps: Kiran could have stayed because the umpire missed it.
He chose honesty over his own score.
Being honest and fair in sport is sportsmanship.
example.answer: It shows honesty and good sportsmanship.

learn.reallife: At the end of every match, players shake hands — a small habit that shows respect, whoever wins.

topics.title: Adverbs: how, when, where, how often

learn.hook: Sana ran FAST, helped KINDLY and played FAIRLY. Those capital words are adverbs — let's meet them!
points: An adverb tells us more about a verb (and sometimes an adjective or another adverb).
Adverbs of manner tell how: quickly, bravely, kindly, carefully. Many are made by adding -ly to adjectives (quick → quickly).
Adverbs of time tell when (now, soon, yesterday); of place tell where (here, there, outside); of frequency tell how often (always, often, sometimes, never).
Some adverbs don't end in -ly: fast, hard, well, late. 'Good' is an adjective; its adverb is 'well' (She plays well).
Careful: 'hardly' means 'almost not'. 'He worked hard' is very different from 'He hardly worked'!

example.q: Think it through: Find the adverbs and what they tell us: 'Yesterday, Sana played bravely outside.'
steps: 'Yesterday' tells when → time.
'bravely' tells how she played → manner.
'outside' tells where → place.
example.answer: yesterday (time), bravely (manner), outside (place)

learn.reallife: Sports commentary is full of adverbs: 'He bowled quickly', 'She always smiles', 'They played well today.'

learn.hook: Who is the real winner — the one who comes first, or the one who never gives up?
points: 'The Winner' is a poem about what it really means to win: effort, courage and not giving up.
A poem can make us rethink a word. Here, 'winning' means doing your best, not only coming first.
Couplets are pairs of lines that rhyme. A poem made of rhyming couplets has the rhyme scheme AABBCC...
Poets use images like 'a fire inside' to show strong feelings such as determination.
Read a poem aloud to feel its rhythm — the beat of strong and soft sounds.

example.q: Read this original poem: I tripped on the track and I heard the loud cheer / For the runners ahead as the finish drew near; / My knees were all scraped and my laces untied, / But I stood up again with a fire inside. / I came in last, but I crossed the line — / And the medal of trying is shining and mine. Why does the speaker feel like a winner?
steps: The speaker tripped, got hurt and came in last.
But they stood up again 'with a fire inside' and crossed the line.
They call their effort 'the medal of trying'.
example.answer: Because they did not give up — they got up and finished the race, and that effort is their 'medal'.

learn.reallife: School sports days give medals to the top three, but everyone who finishes the race has shown courage.

learn.hook: A spider fails seven times to climb its thread and climbs on the eighth. That spider knows a big word: perseverance!
points: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult or takes a long time.
Word family: persevere (verb), perseverance (noun), persevering (adjective). Similar words: determination, persistence, grit.
The opposite of persevering is giving up or quitting.
Proverbs about perseverance: 'Practice makes perfect', 'Slow and steady wins the race', 'Where there's a will, there's a way'.
Perseverance works best with good habits: setting small goals, practising daily and learning from mistakes.

example.q: Think it through: Neha cannot ride her bicycle and falls three times. She asks her brother to hold the seat and practises every evening for a week. Finally she rides alone. Which proverb fits?

learn.reallife: Learning to swim, playing a musical instrument or solving tough maths sums all need perseverance.

learn.hook: 'I CAN win', 'I MUST practise', 'I SHOULD rest' — little helping verbs carry big meanings!
points: Modal verbs are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would.
Can = ability ('I can run fast') or asking informally ('Can I go out?'). Could = past ability ('I could swim at six').
May = polite permission ('May I come in?') or possibility ('It may rain').
Must = something necessary or a strong duty ('You must wear a helmet'). Should = advice ('You should drink water').
After a modal, use the base verb with no 's', 'ed' or 'to': 'She can sing', not 'She can sings' or 'She can to sing'.

example.q: Think it through: Choose the best modal: 'Players ___ follow the rules of the game.' (can / must / may)

learn.reallife: Rules and signs use modals: 'You must wear a seat belt', 'Visitors may take photos', 'You should wash your hands.'

learn.hook: What can make you as steady as a mountain and as calm as a still lake — without any gadgets? Yoga!
points: 'Yoga — A Way of Life' is an informative lesson about yoga and how it helps the body and mind.
The word 'yoga' comes from the Sanskrit root 'yuj', which means 'to join' or 'to unite' — joining body, breath and mind.
Yoga includes asanas (postures), pranayama (breathing exercises) and meditation (quietly focusing the mind).
Benefits: better flexibility, strength and balance, a calmer mind and better concentration.
International Day of Yoga is celebrated every year on 21 June. The United Nations declared it in 2014, and it was first celebrated in 2015.

example.q: Read: Every morning, Kavya unrolls her mat on the terrace. She begins with slow, deep breaths. Then she stands tall like a mountain and stretches like a tree. "Yoga makes my body flexible and my mind calm," she says. Since she started, she finds it easier to concentrate on her studies, and she rarely feels stiff after long hours at her desk. List two benefits of yoga that Kavya mentions or experiences.
steps: Kavya says yoga makes her body flexible.
She says it makes her mind calm.
She finds it easier to concentrate and rarely feels stiff.
example.answer: Any two: a flexible body, a calm mind, better concentration, less stiffness.

learn.reallife: Many schools hold a yoga session on 21 June, and lots of families begin their day with a few asanas and pranayama.

learn.hook: Your body is like a phone: it needs charging (sleep), good fuel (food) and the right apps (exercise)!
points: A healthy lifestyle includes a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep, cleanliness and a calm mind.
A balanced diet has the right amounts of different foods: grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk products and water.
Instructions (like yoga steps) are written as imperative sentences that start with a verb: 'Stand straight.' 'Breathe in slowly.'
Sequence words make instructions clear: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Safety in yoga: practise on a mat with an empty or light stomach, learn from a trained teacher, and never force a pose that hurts.

example.q: Think it through: Turn this into instructions for the tree pose (Vrikshasana): stand straight; raise one foot to the inside of the other leg; join palms; hold; come back.
steps: Begin each step with a verb.

example.answer: First, stand straight. Next, place your right foot on the inside of your left leg (not on the knee). Then join your palms. Hold and breathe. Finally, lower your foot and repeat on the other side.

learn.reallife: Recipes, game rules and science-activity steps are all written as imperative instructions with sequence words.

learn.hook: Some sentences tell, some ask, some order and some shout with joy. Can you tell which is which?
points: A declarative (assertive) sentence makes a statement and ends with a full stop: 'Yoga keeps us fit.'
An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark: 'Do you practise yoga?'
An imperative sentence gives a command, request or instruction: 'Stand straight.' 'Please close the door.'
An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: 'What a lovely morning!'
In imperative sentences the subject 'you' is usually understood, not written.

example.q: Think it through: Identify each: (a) Breathe in deeply. (b) How calm I feel! (c) Is yoga easy? (d) Kavya does yoga daily.
steps: (a) gives an instruction → imperative.
(b) shows strong feeling → exclamatory.
(c) asks → interrogative.
(d) states a fact → declarative.

learn.hook: Travel a few hundred kilometres in India and the language, food and clothes may all change — yet everyone is Indian!
points: 'Hamara Bharat — Incredible India!' is a lesson about the amazing variety of India's land, people and ways of life.
Diversity means variety — many different kinds. India has diversity in languages, food, clothes, festivals, music, dance and landscape.
India has 28 states and 8 union territories. The Constitution lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, and many more are spoken.
Landscapes range from the snowy Himalayas to the Thar Desert in Rajasthan, the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans and long coastlines.
'Unity in diversity' means that, despite our differences, we are united as one nation.

example.q: Read: In Asha's class, Arjun's family is from Punjab, Lalitha's from Tamil Nadu, Joseph's from Kerala and Rinku's from Assam. At lunch, the tiffins open: makki di roti, curd rice, appam and pitha. Arjun says 'Sat Sri Akal', Lalitha says 'Vanakkam' and Rinku says 'Nomoskar'. Different foods, different greetings — one happy class. What does this passage show about India?

Yet they form 'one happy class'.
example.answer: It shows unity in diversity: different foods and languages, but one united class (like one united India).

learn.hook: From Garba nights to Bihu dances and Onam feasts, India celebrates almost every week of the year!
points: Culture is the way of life of a group of people: their language, food, clothes, music, dance, art and festivals.
Traditions are customs and beliefs passed down from one generation to the next.

Classical dances of India include Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathakali (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha) and Manipuri (Manipur). Folk dances include Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Bihu (Assam) and Ghoomar (Rajasthan).
Harvest festivals are celebrated in different ways: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Onam (Kerala), Bihu (Assam), Baisakhi (Punjab).
People of all communities celebrate festivals like Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Guru Nanak Jayanti and Buddha Purnima, and neighbours often join in each other's celebrations.

learn.hook: 'India have many languages' or 'India has many languages'? Let's make subjects and verbs agree!
points: The verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
In the simple present, singular subjects (he, she, it, one name) take verbs with -s/-es: 'Ravi dances.' Plural subjects don't: 'They dance.'
is/was/has go with singular subjects; are/were/have go with plural subjects. 'I am', 'you are' are special.
Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural: 'Asha and Ravi are friends.'
Words like each, every, everyone, everybody take a singular verb: 'Everyone loves Diwali sweets.' 'One of the states is Goa.'

learn.hook: Whoosh! Swoosh! Can you hear a poem? Some poems are made to be heard as much as read!
points: 'The Kites' is a poem about the joy and colour of kites flying in the sky.
Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they describe (whoosh, swoosh, flutter, snap).
Alliteration: the same first sound repeated in words close together ('bright, breezy day').
Personification: kites 'go dancing', as if they were people. A metaphor: 'The sky is a garden.'
Rhyme and rhythm make a poem feel like the swaying, rising and dipping of a kite.

example.q: Read this original poem: Up on the roof on a bright, breezy day, / Red kites and green kites go dancing away; / The string in my hand hums whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, / As up goes my kite with a swoop and a swoosh. / "Kai po che!" shouts my cousin with glee — / The sky is a garden as far as I see. Find one example each of onomatopoeia, alliteration and metaphor.
steps: Sound words: 'whoosh' and 'swoosh' → onomatopoeia.
'bright, breezy' repeat the 'b' sound → alliteration.
'The sky is a garden' calls the sky a garden without 'like' → metaphor.
example.answer: Onomatopoeia: whoosh/swoosh; alliteration: bright, breezy; metaphor: the sky is a garden.

learn.hook: In January, the skies over many Indian cities fill with thousands of kites. Which festival is it?
points: Makar Sankranti, in January, marks the sun's movement into Makara (Capricorn). It is a harvest-time festival celebrated across India by different names.
In Gujarat it is called Uttarayan, and people fly kites from rooftops all day. Ahmedabad hosts a famous International Kite Festival.
In Tamil Nadu the same season brings Pongal; in Punjab, Lohri is celebrated the night before Makar Sankranti; in Assam, it is Magh (Bhogali) Bihu.
Kites are also flown on Independence Day (15 August) in Delhi and other places.
Kite safety: never use glass-coated or nylon string (manja) — it hurts birds and people; stay away from electric wires; fly only from safe places with an adult nearby.

example.q: Think it through: Rehan wants to fly kites on Uttarayan with glass-coated manja from the edge of the roof near an electric wire. What three things should he change?
steps: Glass-coated manja can cut birds and people → use plain cotton thread.
The edge of the roof is dangerous → stay in a safe, railed area with an adult.
Electric wires are dangerous → fly far away from them.
example.answer: Use plain cotton thread, stay in a safe place with an adult, and keep away from electric wires.

learn.reallife: Bird hospitals and volunteers in Gujarat work extra hard during Uttarayan to help birds hurt by sharp manja — safe string saves lives.
